title: Gideon and the Portrait
premise: Seven years after her twin brother Gideon vanished the night their grandmother died, Freya Vane returns to the family house to bury a body identified as his—except she knows it isn't him, because Gideon never left. The house has been keeping something fed, and every photograph now shows an extra chair at the table, waiting. As night falls, Freya uncovers what her grandmother invited in decades ago: a bargain that traded one twin's identity to keep the other alive, and Gideon has been wearing Freya's absence like a skin ever since. To survive until sunrise, Freya must unmake the invitation by claiming the name that was stolen from her, even if it means letting the thing that loved her as a sister take Gideon's place instead.
about_author: Kestrel Brightwater is the pen name of a former funeral home archivist who spent five years cataloguing estate photographs and swears half of them changed between viewings. They write horror about houses that remember, and live alone with a dog who refuses to enter one particular room.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At the funeral home, Freya views the casket and recognizes instantly that the body is not her twin—the hands are wrong, the scar missing. She signs the paperwork anyway, unable to explain why. Emotional beat: guilt curdling into dread; the first lie of many.

chapters.title: Housekeeping
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She arrives at grandma's house to sort the estate, finding it unnervingly maintained—dishes washed, beds made—as if someone still lives there. A neighbor mentions seeing lights for years. Emotional beat: the comfort of home turning unfamiliar.

chapters.title: Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Sorting photographs, she notices every family picture now includes an empty chair pulled up to the table where none was before. The oldest photos show it too. Emotional beat: rationalization straining against evidence.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Saw
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Marisol, the neighbor, recalling seven years of watching a figure in the upstairs window who waved with the wrong hand. She never told anyone. Emotional beat: complicity of silence; the town chose not to know.

chapters.title: Gideon's Room
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The twin's bedroom is untouched but lived-in: fresh laundry, a journal with entries in handwriting that drifts from Gideon's to Freya's own. The last entry reads 'she's coming home.' Emotional beat: violation and vertigo.

chapters.title: The Journal
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Reading backward through the journal, she finds Gideon documenting his own dissolution—forgetting his name, hearing grandmother's voice teaching him 'the arrangement.' Emotional beat: grief reframed as horror; he didn't run, he was kept.

chapters.title: Dinner Invitation
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She finds the table set for two and hears movement upstairs. Instead of fleeing, exhausted and angry, she sits down and says aloud, 'I'm not leaving.' The lights flicker—and stay on. Emotional beat: defiance as first act of power.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In the locked cellar she finds grandmother's ledger: payments recorded in years, names, and teeth—a contract renewed annually since 1962. The final entry, seven years old, lists two names: Gideon Vane, and blank space waiting. Emotional beat: understanding the debt.

chapters.title: Marisol Returns
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Worried after seeing Freya's car still there at dusk, Marisol comes over and confesses everything—the figure, the waves, the year she almost called the police and couldn't make herself dial. Emotional beat: found family beginning; two witnesses choosing each other.

chapters.title: First Knock
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Something knocks politely at the back door, then the front, patient and courteous. Through the window glass she sees nothing, but the door handle turns anyway. It stops at midnight exactly. Emotional beat: terror disciplined by rules—there are rules.

chapters.title: The Arrangement Explained
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The ledger plus the journal reveal the mechanism: grandmother bound a hungry presence to the house, feeding it identity instead of flesh—one twin's selfhood purchased the other's survival. Gideon has been hollowing toward the blank space in the ledger. Emotional beat: horror of love weaponized.

chapters.title: Phone Call
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She calls her mother, who goes silent, then whispers that she always knew—grandmother made her choose which twin to register, and she chose wrong. She begs Freya to burn the house. Emotional beat: generational betrayal; the corruption passed down.

chapters.title: Burning Question
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya tries to burn the ledger; the fire won't catch, and the smoke forms a chair shape. The house retaliates gently—doors vanishing, windows showing morning that isn't real. Emotional beat: powerlessness of force against a bargain freely made.

chapters.title: Upstairs, Finally
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She climbs to Gideon's room and finds him—or what remains: a person-shaped absence wearing her brother's outline, speaking in both their voices. He doesn't want to hurt her. He wants to be her. Emotional beat: heartbreak; the monster is her brother's remnant.

chapters.title: Conversation with a Hollow
chapters.summary: Dual POV, alternating paragraphs. Gideon-thing explains the hunger honestly: it was invited, it kept its side, it only took what was offered. It offers Freya the same deal grandmother got—stay, be safe, be loved, pay yearly. Emotional beat: temptation rendered sympathetic.

chapters.title: Marisol Holds the Line
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Outside, Marisol refuses to leave, standing in the yard with salt and a photograph of the real Gideon from school, calling his true name into the dark. The house screams. Emotional beat: courage of ordinary loyalty; found family tested.

chapters.title: The Name That Was Stolen
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya realizes the blank ledger line isn't for her—it's the vacancy Gideon left when his name was taken. Names can be returned. She begins writing his name back into the record, hand cramping, the house fighting her stroke by stroke. Emotional beat: agency reclaimed through truth-telling.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Completing the entry, she learns the final truth: grandmother never invited a monster. She invited her dead husband, and something else answered the door. The presence isn't evil—it's a guest overstaying a misdirected welcome. Emotional beat: pity replacing fear.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The contract dissolves at dawn, but the guest must be given somewhere to go or it will take the house down with it. Freya offers it the one thing no one did: a proper farewell, a name of its own, spoken with kindness. Emotional beat: compassion as exorcism.

chapters.title: The Letting Go
chapters.summary: Climax, Freya's POV. At 5:47 a.m., Freya speaks the release aloud while Marisol holds the threshold. Gideon's outline fills briefly with light, becomes briefly, truly her brother—he squeezes her hand once—then the extra chair empties forever. The house exhales. Emotional beat: catharsis; grief finally allowed.

chapters.title: Two Coffins
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, weeks later. Freya holds a second, honest funeral and buries the stranger's body under Gideon's name so someone can rest. She keeps one photograph—with the chair—and hangs it by the door as a reminder of what was survived. Emotional beat: mourning completed, identity chosen.

chapters.title: Open House
chapters.summary: Freya and Marisol's shared POV, closing scene. They move into the restored house together, an unlikely household. On the last page, Freya sets the table for three out of habit, smiles, and leaves the third chair empty—not in fear, but in welcome. Emotional beat: found family; the difference between a haunting and a home.
